content.text: Yifan, look how lively it is here! I took a photo—these plush toys are especially popular, and the kids are all gathered around them. It seems our previous survey on idle items was spot-on; toys are indeed one of the most popular categories for exchange.

I see, it really is quite heartwarming. My repair stall has also gotten busy. I just helped an auntie fix her electric kettle, and she was so happy she kept praising how practical it was. This perfectly aligns with the idea of 'making the most of things' we discussed earlier—repairing is more valuable than simply discarding.
Great! I knew your skills would come in handy. By the way, did you bring all the tools you mentioned earlier? I remember the list you made during the planning session last time.

I brought a screwdriver, a multimeter, and soldering wire—the basic tools are all here, so handling these small repairs shouldn’t be a problem. I just taught a dad how to remove rust from the battery contacts of a toy car, and he seemed quite interested. This kind of hands-on sharing is much more intuitive than our previous discussion about "skill sharing" in the planning phase.

Haha, your repair stall is almost turning into a skill-sharing class! Everything’s going smoothly on my end too. The picture book that mom took is just right for her child to read, and we even exchanged WeChat contacts so we can stay in touch and share more in the future. This atmosphere of "mutual help and sharing" is even better than we expected.

Here's a photo of me repairing something for you to see—I was focused on fixing the circuit board. This kind of hands-on demonstration is much more effective than just talking about theory. I remember when we discussed the event format last time, I felt that the hands-on part was really important.

Wow, you're really focused on your work! I remember you mentioned during the last planning session that you wanted to make the most of everything, and now it's clear the results are great. On my end, the item exchange is moving along quickly too—toys and books are the most popular, which aligns perfectly with our earlier survey findings.

Well, efficiency optimization. I've observed that the repair stall has addressed several typical issues: thermostat replacement, contact cleaning, and basic circuit checks. The feedback from residents has been quite positive. It seems our previous estimate of the demand for 'small appliance repairs' was spot on.

I took another photo. Look at the crowd! Parents are picking out toys with their kids, and it's really lively. Our event has instantly boosted the sense of community belonging. Compared to our last planning session, which was just theoretical, seeing everyone actually come together feels incredibly reassuring.

Indeed, the concepts of technological democracy and self-sufficiency can be better disseminated through such activities. The division of labor table you shared earlier was very clear, making today's execution much smoother. From planning to implementation, the process has been optimized effectively.

Thank you for the compliment! My efforts and worries haven't been in vain. The event is almost over, so let's review it. Which items were the most popular, and what improvements can be made to the repair booth? We can also compare these with our initial plans during the planning phase.

Okay. From my perspective, children's toys, small household appliances, and books are the most popular items, which aligns perfectly with our previous survey's "Top 3 Idle Items." As for the repair stalls, we could prepare more illustrated guides for common malfunctions to help residents learn on their own. This can also be seen as an extension of our previous discussion on "skill retention."

Agreed! I think the aspect of mutual aid and sharing is particularly well demonstrated. Look, after that mother took the picture book, she even mentioned donating some old clothes. Should we consider holding these events regularly? Just like we discussed last time, we need to establish a sustainable mechanism.

Holding events regularly has its benefits; it helps form habits and promotes the circulation of items. However, the frequency should be reasonable, such as once per quarter, to avoid fatigue. I suggest adding a skill-sharing segment, like we did today. This takes us a step further than the simple item exchange we initially envisioned.

I've just compiled some follow-up improvement suggestions and sent them to you for review. They include item zoning, skill sharing, and statistical lists. What do you think? These are all based on the actual feedback from today's event and the foundation of our previous planning.

I've read it, and it's very pragmatic. Dividing items into zones can improve efficiency, skill sharing can be extended to residents beyond myself, and statistical lists help optimize resources. If held regularly, all these measures can be utilized. Our planning is being iteratively refined step by step.

Great! Then it's settled, we'll collaborate again for the next event. Your repair skills received a lot of recognition today, so from now on, you'll be our community's 'technical advisor'! From the moment you proposed this idea last time to its successful implementation today, it's truly a perfect full circle.

No problem, it's all about mutual help and sharing. The success of today's event is thanks to your organizational skills and warm-heartedness. From the planning last time to the execution this time, our collaboration has become increasingly seamless. It feels great to see the entire project come together from scratch.

Yes, from the survey on idle items to the successful event now, it feels like the community's warmth has increased. Thank you for your support, Yifan! Before the next event, let's refine our division of labor again, just like this time, to make the planning more solid.

Okay, feel free to reach out anytime. Today was quite fruitful—we not only solved practical problems but also fostered interaction among neighbors. I'll send you the updated tool list and common troubleshooting diagrams later, so you can be better prepared next time. This event really put all our planning ideas from last time to the test.
